title: Lara Croft: Tomb Raider: Cradle of Life
full_review:
At the end of the day there are only two types of moviegoers: those who care if Lara Croft ever finds Pandora's fabled box and those who do not. For those who do, "Lara Croft Tomb Raider: The Cradle of Life" (Paramount) is sheer escapist fun in the tradition of "Raiders of the Lost Ark" with a high-tech feminist twist. For those who do not, director Jan De Bont's video game-inspired sequel amounts to little more than a ridiculous exercise in excess whose hokey, long-winded title alone will have their highbrow hands reaching for a copy of Proust.

Whatever the case may be, this film -- which is nearly as long as Lara's signature ponytail -- while a marked upgrade from the 2001 original, deviates little from the prefab high-octane paradigm of its predecessor.

For those viewers who actually like a bone tossed to their cerebral cortexes while their adrenal glands are served a nine-course feast, fear not: Somewhere amid the slow-motion ammo clips, there is a plot. Lara Croft, (Angelina Jolie) the buxom British archeologist and adventurer -- think Indiana Jones with a Wonderbra -- must find the legendary box of Pandora before it falls into the sinister clutches of Dr. Jonathan Reiss (Ciaran Hinds), who plans to use it in one of those deliciously diabolical world domination schemes that make these films so much fun.

In case you forgot your Greek mythology, Pandora was a woman to whom the gods gave a box which contained all the evils not yet present in the world. Despite stern warnings to the contrary, she opened the lid, releasing pestilence, suffering and telemarketers. In this version, the box contains a power known only as "anti-life," which if unleashed will destroy all living things on Earth. Tied up in all this is an orb-shaped map that reveals the box's well-guarded resting place inside an African volcano, known as the "Cradle of Life." Along for the globetrotting roller-coaster ride is ex-British commando turned mercenary bad-boy Terry Sheridan (Gerard Butler), who had been romantically involved with the voluptuous daredevil.

With all the bullets flying some were bound to hit the screenplay, which is riddled with narrative holes, not to mention logical and logistical lapses big enough to drive Lara's Hummer through. An alternative title might be "Lara Croft Plot Raider" since much of its unabashedly derivative story has been swiped from such genre precursors as "Raiders of the Lost Ark" and "King Solomon's Mines."

Yet while it has maintained Indiana Jones' bullwhip veneer, it has jettisoned the key ingredient in the "Raiders" recipe for success: hinge the action on a well-developed character. Sure, Indy hopped from Tunis to Tibet looking for lost loot, but he occasionally ran into a snake and showed some vulnerability. Lara, despite being saddled with a forced romantic subplot in an attempt to prove there is a pulse under that icy glare and those ripped abs, still comes across as little more than a video-game adolescent fantasy.

That being said, Jolie is electric as every misogynist's worst nightmare, the perfect blend of feminine charm and bare-knuckle moxie, tough enough to slug it out with the boys while dainty enough to ride sidesaddle, injecting the role with a refreshing sense of tongue-in-cheek humor. While some may justifiably be concerned that her testosterone-tinged temperament may not present the best role model for young women -- unlike the troika of bimbos in "Charlie's Angels" -- Lara Croft uses her brain as much as her fists and never exploits her sexuality. She also operates with a clear view of right and wrong, sacrificing wealth and personal gain in order to follow the dictates of her conscience.

Of course, her conscience has little to say about the body count she cavalierly racks up during the repetitive, consequence-free shoot-'em-ups which occupy most of the screen time, betraying the flick's violent video-game pedigree.

One thing smuggled under the radar is a materialistic view of creation. In one scene Lara explains how all life sprang from a primordial soup sparked by the energy in the sought-after box. The film also suggests a subtle but dangerous dualistic philosophy, claiming that light and darkness, good and evil, pain and pleasure are but two complementary -- read equal -- sides of the same coin.

"Cradle of Life" proves that, while much of what flew out of Pandora's box has a Hollywood mailing address, every once in a while Tinseltown can churn out a mindless movie that's fun to watch.

Due to much action violence, brief sensuality and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
